extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students of analytic geometry (19th‑century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations and necessary/sufficient conditions for geometric properties of second‑degree surfaces (quadrics), tangent planes, and many classical properties and constructions for the ellipse (parametrisation, chords, tangents, inscribed/circumscribed polygons, sector/area relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: General equation of a surface of the second degree
rubrics_metrics.description: The general equation to surfaces of the second degree may be written in the canonical form u = Ax^2 + By^2 + Cz^2 + Dx + Ey + Fz + Q = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the starting canonical form for all subsequent reductions, substitutions, and classifications of quadrics in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface through intersections of two planes (construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two planes cutting a surface are V = ax + βy + γz + 1 = 0 and V' = a'x + β'y + γ'z + 1 = 0, then the equation of any surface of second degree passing through their two intersection curves can be written as u = m·V·V' (m arbitrary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to generate a one‑parameter family of quadrics that pass through the same pair of plane intersection curves; expand and compare coefficients to find special members (e.g., spheres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for the auxiliary surface to be a sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: When the constructed surface u = m V V' is a sphere, the expanded coefficient equalities give specific linear relations among the plane coefficients and the quadric coefficients (system (d)); generally inconsistent unless some plane coefficients vanish, yielding special subcases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper analyses the system and shows which coefficient vanishing choices produce a sphere or other special surfaces (see subsequent special‑case items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Every quadric has six series of circular sections (in general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general every surface of the second degree has six series of circular sections (real or imaginary) parallel to the three principal axes of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a global classification statement deduced from the equations (Ji), (ftj), (fcj); the reality or imaginarity of the series depends on the signs and relative sizes of principal coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of circular section planes from linear/constant terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of the planes that give circular sections depends only on the quadratic coefficients (A, B, C) and is independent of the linear coefficients D, E, F and the absolute term G (Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus translations (D,E,F) do not change the orientation of circular section planes; only principal quadratic terms matter for the directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsoid case — two real series of circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: When the given surface is an ellipsoid (principal axes chosen so equation is A x^2 + B y^2 + C z^2 = 1 with A,B,C>0 and A < B < C), two of the families given by the derived equations are real and indicate two series of real circular sections parallel to the axis of y or to the mean axis of the ellipsoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes which of the three sets of solutions are real versus imaginary for given orderings of A,B,C and hence which axes yield real circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperboloid of one sheet — two real circular series
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hyperboloid of one sheet (principal form with G negative and suitable ordering A, B), only two series of real circular sections occur; both series are parallel to the greater axis of the principal elliptic section (the greater real axis of the surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis of which of the three solution sets are real gives this conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperboloid of two sheets — two real circular series (imaginary axis orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hyperboloid of two sheets (principal form with particular ordering), two series of circular sections are real and their planes are both parallel to the y‑axis or the greater imaginary axis of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again determined by which solution sets yield real values for the plane coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic paraboloid — two real circular series parallel to one axis
rubrics_metrics.description: An elliptic paraboloid (referred to its axis and principal diametral planes so that equation is B y^2 + C z^2 − a x = 0 with A=0) has two series of circular sections, both parallel to the axis of y which lies in the plane of the principal parabolic section whose parameter is the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two of the three formulaic solution sets become imaginary; the remaining pair gives the two real series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic paraboloid — nominal circular series degenerate to lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyperbolic paraboloid has two formal series of circular sections parallel to the principal axis, but each 'circle' degenerates into a straight line (intersection projects to straight lines on coordinate planes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elimination shows intersections project as straight lines, so planar 'circles' are degenerate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone — two series of circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: A quadric cone (in principal axes) has two series of circular sections (when A < B the corresponding solution set is real), the others imaginary; these are parallel to the axis x or to the greater axis of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar reality/imaginarity analysis to the above cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic cylinder — two real series parallel to principal axis
rubrics_metrics.description: An elliptic cylinder (principal form A x^2 + B y^2 = 1) has two series of circular sections parallel to the greater axis of the principal section (when A < B one of the solution sets is real).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cylinder reduces the general three‑axis analysis to two nonzero quadratic coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic cylinder — 'circles' degenerate into lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyperbolic cylinder yields equations that appear to indicate two series of circular sections, but as with the hyperbolic paraboloid the circles degenerate into straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again verified by projection/elimination arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic cylinder — all planar perpendicular sections nominally circles but degenerate
rubrics_metrics.description: A parabolic cylinder reduced to the form B y^2 − a x = 0 gives that every section by a plane perpendicular to the y‑axis is a 'circle' in the algebraic sense, but each of these circles degenerates into a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algebraic solution set for the circularity condition collapses to linear factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface of revolution condition (special coefficient vanishing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a = a' = β = β' = 0 in the plane coefficients appearing in the circularity system, then the reduced relations give B = A and the remaining plane coefficients arbitrary; in this case the surface must be a surface of revolution and the circular section planes are perpendicular to the axis of revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent special choices of which plane coefficients vanish (several symmetric possibilities) yield the same conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere condition (all principal quadratic coefficients equal)
rubrics_metrics.description: If additionally y = y' = a = a' = β = β' = 0 (i.e., sufficient vanishing so that the reduced system gives A = B = C), then the surface is a sphere and the planes of circular section are indeterminate (every plane section is a circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sphere arises as the fully symmetric special case A = B = C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for coordinate planes to be tangential to a quadric (traces degenerate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The coordinate planes are tangential to the surface when each of the traces of the surface on the coordinate planes denotes a point or a line; algebraically this gives determinant/degeneracy conditions among the trace coefficients (equations analogous to (5),(6),(7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These determinant equalities (conic degeneracy conditions) are the necessary and sufficient relations for tangency to all three coordinate planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General equation of a second‑order surface referred to three tangent planes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quadric is described relative to three tangent planes, its general equation can be written Az^2 + By^2 + Cz^2 + 2d yz + 2e xz + 2f xy + 2g z + 2h y + 2k x + 1 = 0 with the quadratic and linear coefficients expressible by explicit combinations of the tangency parameters (expressions given in the paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper provides explicit (albeit heavy) formulae for the coefficients in terms of the tangency constants; students are invited to verify sign choices when substitution yields a non‑quadric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centres of inscribed and circumscribed second‑order surfaces in a parallelepiped coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: If surfaces of the second order are inscribed in a given parallelepiped and also others circumscribed about the same parallelepiped, then all these inscribed and circumscribed surfaces have the same centre, which is also the centre of the circumscribed surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by expressing tangency conditions to three faces and eliminating parameters to find X, Y, Z of the centre in closed form (equations (18)–(20)); presented as a novel property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse parametrisation by eccentric anomaly
rubrics_metrics.description: A point P on ellipse of semiaxes a (major) and b (minor) can be parametrised as x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ where θ is the eccentric anomaly (angle on auxiliary circle described on major axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parametrisation simplifies many subsequent chord, tangent, sector, and area formulae and is explicitly recommended as advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of chord between two ellipse points (in eccentric anomaly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chord through points with eccentric anomalies θ_i and θ_j has the neat form (derived): (y/ b)·(sin(θ_i) + sin(θ_j)) − (x/ a)·(cos(θ_i) + cos(θ_j)) = cos(θ_i) cos(θ_j) − sin(θ_i) sin(θ_j) (as given by equation (2) in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This chord formula is used to deduce tangent equation (limit θ_i→θ_j) and midline/radius bisector equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chord length formula in eccentric anomaly
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of chord P_i P_j is given by P_iP_j = 2 sin((θ_j − θ_i)/2)·√{ a^2 sin^2((θ_i+θ_j)/2) + b^2 cos^2((θ_i+θ_j)/2) } (equation (3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for area bounds and polygon side computations; specialisations give simpler relations for symmetric configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of tangent at P (derived from chord formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking θ_i → θ_j in the chord formula gives the tangent at P with eccentric anomaly θ as (x/ a) cos θ + (y/ b) sin θ = 1 (tangent linear equation as presented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tangent equation yields further geometric results: normal relations, conjugate diameter constructions, and tangent intersection properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugate diameters relation and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: If OP and OF are conjugate radii with eccentric anomalies θ and θ', then tan θ' = −cot θ = tan(±(π/2 − θ)); explicit coordinate relations for the conjugate point are given: x' = ±(a sin θ) = ±(a sin θ), y' = ±(b cos θ) = ±x (equation (8) style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives geometric construction: project perpendicular from P to major axis to circle, reflect, and map back to ellipse to obtain conjugate point/diameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of squares of conjugate radii
rubrics_metrics.description: For conjugate radii r and r' (parallel and conjugate) one has r^2 + r'^2 = a^2 + b^2 (equation (10)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in deriving extremal and metric properties of radii and polygons inscribed in the ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse–circle sector and segment proportionalities
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a proportional relationship between corresponding elements on the auxiliary circle and the ellipse: an elliptic sector PiOPj equals (b/a) times the corresponding circular sector QiOQj; likewise elliptic segments correspond proportionally (statements (15)–(17)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proportionality underlies constructions for dividing the ellipse into equal sectors and transfers many regular polygon properties from the circle to the ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction to divide ellipse into n equal sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a regular n‑gon is inscribed in the auxiliary circle on the major axis and perpendiculars dropped to the major axis meet the ellipse at P_i, the radial sectors P_i O P_{i+1} divide the ellipse into n equal sectors (construction (D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a circle can be divided into equal arcs (when constructible), this yields an indefinite number of ways to divide the ellipse into n equal sectors; practical constructibility depends on dividing the circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum inscribed polygon criterion (ellipse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n, an inscribed polygon in the ellipse has maximal area exactly when the corresponding polygon in the auxiliary circle is regular; consequently an infinite family of maximal polygons exist corresponding to rotations of the regular n‑gon (statement (E)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Area formula: maximal inscribed polygon area = (1/2) a b n sin(2π/n) (equation (22) style). Construction uses projecting regular circular polygon points to the ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of maximum polygon tangents (F & G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polygon inscribed in the ellipse is maximum, the tangent at any vertex P_m is parallel to the chord joining the two vertices adjacent to the opposite vertex (i.e., tangent at P_m parallel to chord P_{m−1}P_{m+1}); conversely, if every vertex tangent is parallel to the opposite bisecting chord then the polygon is maximal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic condition on eccentric anomalies reduces to 0_{m−1} + 0_{m+1} = 2 0_m (mod appropriate period) — used to characterise extremals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special hexagon property (H)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a maximal inscribed hexagon in an ellipse each side equals the radius parallel to it (geometric equality between side length and parallel radius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogue of a Euclidean corollary; derived from trigonometric identities when n=6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationships between inscribed polygon and corresponding circle polygon areas (21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Area of any polygon inscribed in the ellipse equals (b/a) times the area of the corresponding polygon inscribed in the auxiliary circle (equation (21)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus extremal properties in the circle carry over, scaled, to the ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum circumscribed polygon criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given n, a polygon formed by tangents at points P_i (obtained by projecting the vertices of a regular n‑gon on the circle) is a minimum circumscribed polygon about the ellipse; its area equals a^2 n tan(π/n) / ? (formula given in paper style, see (37)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: find P_i as in (D), draw tangents at P_i and take their intersections; corresponding regular polygon in circumscribing circle yields minimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of angular points of minimum circumscribed polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed n, the locus of angular points of all minimum polygons circumscribing the ellipse is a concentric similar ellipse whose semiaxes are a sec(π/n) and b sec(π/n) (statement (N)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinates of tangent intersection points and their angular parameters are given in the text (equation (38) etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum quadrilateral circumscribing ellipse is parallelogram touching conjugate diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimum quadrilateral circumscribing an ellipse touches it at the extremities of conjugate diameters; its sides are parallel and equal to these diameters, hence every minimum circumscribing quadrilateral is a parallelogram (statement (R)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is obtained by specialising the general n‑gon results to n=4 and using conjugate diameter relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sides of a minimum circumscribing polygon are bisected at points of contact
rubrics_metrics.description: For any minimum circumscribing polygon about an ellipse, the sides are bisected at the points where they touch the ellipse (statement (S)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General property following from symmetry and the eccentric‑angle relations among vertices and tangent points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum‑of‑squares property for vertices of maximal polygon (I)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from any point S in space lines are drawn to the vertices of a maximal n‑gon inscribed in an ellipse, the sum of the squares of those distances equals n times a quantity: half the sum of squares of the semiaxes plus the square of the distance of S from the centre (equation (27)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalises property (26) and provides a neat invariant for maximal polygons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent plane at a point of an algebraic surface (linearisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface of order n given by F(x,y,z)=0 (expanded about a point (x_i,y_i,z_i)), the tangent plane at that point is obtained by linearising the shifted equation: ax + by + cz = 1 (equation (13)), where a, b, c are the first derivative‑type coefficients evaluated at the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation uses binomial expansions after translating origin to the point; condition (12) relates linear coefficients of the plane to trace tangency conditions on coordinate plane traces. If all linear coefficients vanish at a point, the point is singular and the tangents do not lie in one plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular point criterion for tangent planes
rubrics_metrics.description: The linear tangent‑plane equation fails when, for particular values of x_i, y_i, z_i, all coefficients of the variables vanish; then (x_i,y_i,z_i) is a singular point and the rectilinear tangents at that point need not lie in a single plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singularity detected by vanishing of first‑order coefficients in the expansion; classical criterion for non‑smooth points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collineation coordinate transformation (geometric derivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper gives a geometrical construction for corresponding points under a collinear (collineation) mapping and derives the analytic relations between coordinates in the two systems; the resulting coordinate transformation has the fractional‑linear form obtained by eliminating parameters (equation (6) form and later general forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: intersect corresponding lines, use ratios along axes to determine images; the analytic form matches the transformation by coordinate change and demonstrates equivalence of geometric and algebraic treatments.
